I noticed that in this job, where only a deep category theory file on galois theory was changed by the new commit, CI failed to get the cache. (Note that CI failed on the prior attempt, but still uploaded a cache for most of Mathlib on my fork, which I was able to fetch and use locally.)

Is this expected for security reasons?

Also tagging @Marcelo Lynch :)
This is the downside of the new scoped-by-SHA behavior of the cache: susbequent commits on the same PR do not share the cache, each push acts as if it were 'the first' and only sees cache from master

Gotcha, as long as it's intentional! :grinning_face_with_smiling_eyes: I don't know anything about security but I trust that this is actually a good thing :) (I think actually I knew about this, and then forgot, sorry about that...)
No problem. It's a bad thing for CI perf :-). The point is that this cross-commit sharing would allow a malicious author to poison innocent-looking revisions with earlier-evil-revision-artifacts

@Marcelo Lynch, the new behavior is a major usability regression. Is it possible to mitigate it by allowing the user to mark forks as "trusted"? Eg trusting my own fork would make the new behavior almost indistinguishable from the previous one while providing the same level of security as the new behavior.
@Yaël Dillies You can always use --unsafe to fetch the cache from the latest available commit(s) in your branch history.
We can consider the 'trusted repo' approach as an additional --unsafe option. It's not quite trivial (it needs more metadata in the cache / requests / roundtrips) but it's not terrible either.
I didn't know/overlooked the --unsafe flag, this will do for now thanks!
I'll probably open a PR for the other feature after #41707 is merged

Just spotted this old thread while trying to work out why CI was repeatedly re-building from scratch on my PR's.

I share the sense that this is a quite significant performance / usability regression, particularly in the (quite common) case when you have a PR which modifies a fairly basal mathlib file and then want to deal with fallout in files far downstream of that.

The current situation seems to be, "cache generated by CI builds on forks is never used by CI itself" (but it is available for users to use locally). I can see that this cache-poisoning issue would be a major security concern if cache from fork CI builds were later used for CI on master.

But is it possible to allow CI runs on forks to use cache generated by previous CI runs on the same fork? Then we would re-gain much of the performance loss, while still preventing malicious users from poisoning anything but themselves.

"would be a major security concern if cache from fork CI builds were later used for CI on master"

The security motivation is that reviewers will call 'lake exe cache get' standing on a checked out PR, for review purposes, and so they can get poisoned by a "fork-global" cache universe that was maliciously crafted by the PR author (say, with previous evil unnoticed draft PRs)

It's not my decision to make, but some alternatives include:

(1) making CI use this fork-global cache always, for faster builds, and then if reviewers are wary of security but still want the cache they can kick off a 'commit-scoped' build and then download the artifacts with that scope. This depends on reviewers remembering to do this (which is not an ideal attitude to take towards security), and even in that case it adds friction to the review process (the reviewer needs to wait for CI instead of starting to review right away).

(2) allowlisting a subset of 'trusted' forks to enjoy this fork-global cache. This establishes a different trust boundary for those designated forks that reviewers need to be aware of.
I see, I hadn't thought about the risk to PR reviewers. Thanks for clarifying!

np! Improving build times and the caching model and infrastructure is a priority for me at the MI, so I'm happy to hear any feedback on it. But yes, we are erring on the side of security rather than speed in this situation.
